doc.title: Tony Parenti and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-06-29

title: Fanatza's end and the Stein band's split in Chicago
summary: Finishing the Fanatza story, then Stein's band, the Nunez and Shields changes and Edwards writing to Parenti.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: play the bass with you, I'll go buy one on time. I said okay I'll take you over to the World Line Music Store and I did. We got a big sousaphone for him and he brought it down to his job. He had it in traction high, he had it hung up so that all he had to do was get into this big part of it. A bell. And he'd stand up and play. And he played with him. And he was a member of that little band of mine for many, for the entire length of time at the La Vida, which from there his reputation became known and they became a part of the Sang Amusement Company over the Sanga Theater. And he became, I would say, I don't mean to be mercenary, but he saved his money. Yeah, he is. And he raised his family very nicely. They got out of that neighborhood. They got a beautiful home. In fact, they bought a home. And there's many, many other instances about him. But the reason why I brought that up now is the fact that he always had the greatest admiration for me for giving him his start. And every time I went to New Orleans to see him, he couldn't do enough for me by inviting me home and whining and dining with me. In fact, I've got a picture of him and I together somewhere in my album. And he just passed away of reason. Right, Alan? That's right. And the reason why I brought him up is because he was one of my very favorite musicians at that time who played the finest tuba. Well, they're a real pro. Real tuba. Yes, real pro. And he had a tremendous faculty of being able to play with fine rhythmic value and for not being a jazz man from the beginning, his beat was wonderful. He was always on the beat and any note he took all came out nice and clear and tuned. Yeah, he had the knack of playing good. That's it. You know, old Chick Martin is one of our favorites all the time. Yeah. But this, you have us talk to Chick Martin about Mario Fanacci, he'll tell you the same thing. Only thing, he didn't play string bass. No, that's it. Yeah. He said string bass. But Tony, let me ask you now, when you first left to go to Chicago with the Dixieland band, now the reason why I'm bringing this up is because there's a little pro and con about certain things. Now, going back as a reminder to the fact when I worked at the Pop Cabaret, there was a piano player named Roy Barton I told you about, they had a drummer named Johnny Stein. Yeah. One of the half-brother of Emile. Emile. Johnny was with the band, sure. Well his name, he goes under the name of Johnny Hunter. That's his name. Right? Now Johnny and I have known each other during that particular early time, so thereby, one time, after you fellas had left and went to Chicago, something happened. So Johnny Stein and the other Nunes and the group went up there and something happened. Now whatever happened was that Johnny Stein left and Yola Nunes left. That meant you replaced Johnny Stein and And Eroshield replaced Yola Nunes, right? Well, I'll tell you. I'll tell you the exact situation on that. Johnny Stein was in the band, in the original group. You understand? Yeah. He left for them. In fact, it was Stein's band. Well, that's what I thought. It was Stein's band from Dixieland. It wasn't called the original yet. That's the original band that went up there. That's the original. Yola Nunes, Regis, Edwards, Nicola Rocca and Stein. That was the fight. Now, so they had no sooner gotten up there. In a short while, Edwards started writing to me. For this reason, I had been playing with Giordina, with Edwards. If you remember, I keep saying that Giordina had the best band and Edwards was always the king of a trombone. Him and Brunestown, it was always terrific. That's right. All right. Henry.
Henry. I want to get that straight. There's so many out.
